tagline: The physical layer of IT — pull the cable, mount the gear, and make the connection actually exist.
what_you_do: You build and repair the physical infrastructure every network runs on: pulling and terminating cable, testing and certifying runs, installing and maintaining telecom and transmission equipment, mounting antennas, and restoring service after storms and outages. It's hands-on, on-site work — a van, a tool bag, and a ticket queue instead of a desk. This is one of the few legitimate no-degree, no-coding entries into IT, and it maps almost directly onto military signal and comms experience.
day_in_life: Load the van and drive to the first site — a new office buildout that needs forty cable drops pulled and terminated
Punch down and label each run, then certify it with a cable tester and document the results
Troubleshoot a dead jack by tracing it from the wall plate back through the patch panel
Climb a ladder to mount an access point or antenna and route its cable cleanly
Get pulled off schedule for an outage call — find the damaged span, splice or re-terminate, and restore service

salary.growth: Flat overall (-1 to -3%) as buildouts mature; the tower/wireless branch is the growing exception at ~7%+
salary.note: U.S. BLS figure for Telecom Equipment Installers & Repairers (49-2022); Radio/Cellular/Tower Installers (49-2021) median a similar $63,520. A median is the midpoint of everyone employed, so entry pay runs lower. Verify against the live BLS pages before deciding.

downsides: This is physical work: ladders, crawl spaces, attics in summer, weather that doesn't care about your schedule. Storm and outage restoration means on-call and long days when things break. It is not remote — ever. And the pay ceiling is lower than office IT unless you deliberately move toward network engineering or specialized fiber/tower work.

fits_if: You'd rather work with your hands than sit at a desk all day
You like finishing something you can physically see and test
You want into IT without a degree or any coding
less_ideal_if: You want remote or hybrid work — this is on-site by definition
Physical labor, heights, or weather exposure is a dealbreaker
You want the highest long-term pay ceiling without changing roles later

skills.name: PC & hardware fundamentals
skills.note: Components, connectors, safe handling — the base layer of all field-service work.

skills.name: Copper cabling: pulling, terminating, testing
skills.note: Cat5e/Cat6 runs, punch-downs, RJ45 ends, and reading a cable tester.

skills.name: Structured troubleshooting in the field
skills.note: Isolate the fault: jack, run, patch panel, or the gear behind it.

skills.name: Safety practices (ladders, lifts, PPE, site rules)
Networking fundamentals (IP, switches, Wi-Fi)
skills.note: The bridge skill — this is what turns a cable tech into a network tech.

certs.title: CompTIA A+
certs.reason: Proves the hardware and troubleshooting fundamentals field-service work is built on.

cert_note: Certs matter less here than demonstrable hands-on skill — many techs are hired with none and trained on the job. The industry-specific signals are BICSI's cabling installation certs (Installer 1 and up) and the Fiber Optic Association's certs (CFOT) for fiber work; we don't have guides for those yet, so check their official sites. CompTIA A+ is the one broad cert that helps, mainly for the hardware/field-service side and for pivoting into office IT later.

trial.objective: Feel the hardware side of the job: open a spare desktop, identify every component, then reseat and reassemble it safely.
trial.disclosure: Your own hardware only, power disconnected. No spare machine? Follow a free iFixit teardown guide instead — or spend $15–25 on an Ethernet crimp kit to try the cabling side for real.

roadmap.title: Learn hardware and cabling basics
roadmap.focus: Study A+ material (free via Professor Messer) while getting your hands dirty: tear down a PC, crimp your own Ethernet cables, learn the connector types by touch.

roadmap.title: Prove the fundamentals
roadmap.focus: Earn CompTIA A+ to show hardware and troubleshooting competence — useful for field-service roles and essential if you later pivot indoors.

roadmap.title: Get on a crew
roadmap.focus: Apply to low-voltage contractors, ISPs, and telecom field-service outfits — helper and installer roles hire on attitude and basic skills, and train the rest. Military signal experience slots straight in here. BICSI Installer 1 is the industry credential worth pursuing once you're working.

roadmap.title: Specialize or climb
roadmap.focus: Pick a branch: fiber (FOA CFOT — the higher-skill, better-paid copper alternative), tower/wireless work (the growing segment), or add Network+ knowledge and move into network administration — the classic route to a higher ceiling.

adjacent_paths.reason: Cabling and field work is the classic hands-on route into network engineering.
The office-side twin — same troubleshooting instinct, indoors.
